nodes.question: Which solution was used to adjust the pH to alkaline after pouring the mixture into ice-cold water?
nodes.answer: A saturated sodium acetate solution was used to adjust the pH to alkaline.
nodes.paragraph: Upon completion of the reac - tion, the mixture was poured into 100 mL of ice-cold water, and the pH was adjusted to alkaline by adding a saturated sodium acetate solution, followed by extraction with dichlo - romethane. The pale-yellow liquid, once viscous, solidified upon standing at room temperature to synthesize the alde - hyde ( 3). Yield: 70%, pale yellow solid; mp 63 65 C; lit. mp: 60 62 C [ 27]. Synthesis of 9-ethyl-9 H-carbazole-3,6- dicarbaldehyde (6) Drops of freshly distilled POCI3 (15 mL, 160 mmol) were added to a stirred solution of dry DMF (10 mL, 129 mmol) in a 50 mL two-neck RB flask at 0 C under an argon atmo - sphere until the colored Vilsmeier salt was completely formed. Gradually, while stirring and maintaining a temper - ature of 100 C for 48 h, a solution of 0.50 g (2.60 mmol), of 9-ethyl-9 H-carbazole was added to the reaction mixture in 10 mL of DMF solvent. It was subsequently poured into a mixture of ice and water, and the pH was elevated to an alkaline level using a saturated sodium acetate solution.

nodes.question: How was the soil classified in the northern section where winter wheat was grown?
nodes.answer: The soil in the northern section was classified as silt loam with a pH of 7.
nodes.paragraph: The precrop grown on the field site in the year before the experiment was winter barley (Hordeum vulgare L.). The soil at the site is classified as luvisol devel- oped from loess. For the experiment, the field was split in two sections to grow two different crops winter wheat (WW, Triticum aestivum L.) and Sugar beet (SB, Beta vulgaris L.). Although the two sections were only ~ 10 m apart, soil texture and pH were slightly different. The more northern WW section was classified as silt loam (19% sand, 60% silt, 21% clay) with a pH (CaCI2) of 7, while the more southern SB section was classified as silty clay loam (SB: 23% sand, 49% silt, 29% clay) with a pH (CaCI2) of 7.5. nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What was done to the hydrolyzed root tips right before examination?
nodes.answer: The hydrolyzed root tips were cut and squashed between a slide and a cover slip in a drop of 45% acetic acid before examination.
nodes.paragraph: Seeds were germinated on filter paper in Petri dishes, control groups were moistened with distilled water, and both groups were grown as factorial experi - ment under completely randomized design with three replications at 25 C. Washed root tips of 2 cm, from each treatment were fixed in a 3:1 (v/v) ethanol/glacial acetic acid mixture for 24 h and finally stored at 4 C in a 70% ethanol solution. Fixed root tips were hydrolyzed in 1N HCI at 60 C for 10 min right before examination, and the hydrolysis solution was then replaced by Feulgen stain for around 3 4 h as described in Darlington and La Cour [28]. After being cut and squashed between a slide and a cover in a drop of 45% acetic acid, the strongly stained meristematic region was examined under a light micro - scope at a magnification of 1000 times. A total of 5000 cells from both the control and treatment concentrations were scored. By dividing the number of dividing cells by the total number of cells tested, the mitotic index (M.I.) was computed as a percentage, as well as the percent - ages of mitotic phases.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Soil health management|Soil ph balancing_qna_004
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the pH of the soil at the Swift Current site?
nodes.answer: The pH of the soil at the Swift Current site is 6.5 (measured at a 1:2 ratio of soil to water).
nodes.paragraph: The same study was repeated from 2011 to 2018 at the Crop Diversification Centre, Brooks (50 33 N; 111 53 W; elevation: 747m), Alberta, Canada. Both sites are located in the Mixed Grassland Ecoregion of Canada, in an area where Brown Chernozem soils are prevalent. The soil (0 15 cm) at Swift Current is a silt loam, with 31% sand, 51% silt, and 18% clay, whereas at Brooks the soil (0 15 cm) is a sandy loam, with 46% sand, 32% silt, and 22% clay. At the initiation of this study, soil in the 0 15 cm layer at the Swift Current site had a pH (1:2 ratio of soil to water) of 6.5, bulk density of 1.3 g cm 3, organic carbon (dry combustion after removing inorganic using 6 M HCI) of 10.6 g kg 1, mineral N (2 M KCI extractable N) of 3.4 mg kg 1, and Olsen P (0.5 M NaHCO3) of 26.5 mg kg 1.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What was the pH of the soil at Brooks?
nodes.answer: The pH of the soil at Brooks was 7.8.
nodes.paragraph: The soil at Brooks had a pH of 7.8, soil bulk density of 1.2 g cm 3, organic carbon of 9.9 g kg 1, mineral N of 7.4 mg kg 1, and Olsen P of 82.5 mg kg 1. Both sites were equipped with an on-site weather station for precipitation and tem- perature measurements. The 30-year climate normal data were retrieved from Environment Canada weather stations. At Swift Current, average annual precipitation during the 8-year study period was 401 mm (Table S1), higher than the 1991 2020 climate normal of 394 mm (ECCC 2024), with 250 mm occurring during the typical growing season (May to August). At Brooks, annual precipitation averaged from 2011 to 2018 was 288 mm, slightly below the 1991 2020 climate normal of 299 mm (ECCC 2024), with 177 mm occurring from May to August (Table S1). nodes.question: What was the effect of pH stability when using TMEDA and DACH in cultivation?
nodes.answer: The use of TMEDA and DACH mitigated pH fluctuations compared to the control.
nodes.paragraph: (2023)15 investigated suspended cultivation of Chlorella sp. with 1 15 mM of TMEDA and DACH. It was found that TMEDA inhibited cell growth at higher than 1 mM, while DACH at 1 15 mM remained biomass concentration equivalent to the control without inhibitory effects. Regarding pH stability, the use of these amines mitigated pH fluctuations compared to the control. The diurnal increase in pH also indicated active metabolic processes in the microalgae. Chlorella sp. demonstrated superior carbon storage and conversion efficiency when cultured with DACH at all tested concentrations, outperforming the control, but TMEDA enhanced carbon conversion efficiency was observed only at 1 mM, with no improvement at higher concentrations15. Li et al. (2023)24 investigated the effects of induced TEA into Coccomyxa subellipsoidea cultures using batch and fed-batch systems. The results showed that adding TEA at a concentration of 100 mg/L enhanced CO2 bio-fixation by 1.28-fold and 1.97-fold in the batch and fed-batch systems, respectively, compared to cultures without TEA supplementation. Furthermore, TEA contributed to stabilizing the pH of the culture system and facilitated the conversion of CO2 into HCO3 .
